title: Maria Ressa Maps AI's Path From Feeds to Stolen Agency
seo_title: Maria Ressa Warns Agentic AI Will Steal Agency
excerpt: In Oslo, Nobel laureate Maria Ressa told Reuters that artificial intelligence has already seized attention through social feeds, then intimacy through chatbots, and is now reaching for agency itself through systems that act for us. She put a clock on the tip: without citizen pressure for legislation, control slips. She waved off the China-race veto as "good spin" and said the first repair is liability for past harm. Against a week of lab pledges to pace and contain, her frame is civic. The machines are not waiting for a club deal.
hero_alt: Silhouette of a hand sliding a paper ballot into a ballot box against a bright white backdrop
paragraphs: Maria Ressa did not travel to Oslo to admire the frontier. Speaking during a conference on threats to democracy, the Nobel Peace Prize laureate told Reuters that artificial intelligence has already seized attention through social media, then intimacy through chatbots, and is now reaching for agency itself. The machines she fears are the ones that "don't just pretend to be human, but act for us."

That third wave is the story. Ressa, co-chair of the United Nations' international scientific panel on AI, put a clock on it: if citizens fail to force legislation now, "we will tip" into a phase "beyond our control." She treated the China-race veto, including from the White House, as "good spin," and said Beijing already builds more citizen safeguards into products like TikTok than Silicon Valley ships to the rest of the world.
## Public safety, not a speech quarrel

"It is not a freedom of speech issue to ask for regulation. It's a public safety issue," she said. The line matters because the industry's favorite dodge still pretends every limit is a muzzle. Ressa's sequence runs the other way: first make companies responsible for damage already done, then pressure politicians, then build public-interest platforms outside the feed. She welcomed U.S. lawsuits that pushed Meta toward an $18 billion teen-safety settlement and stricter youth limits on Facebook and Instagram, and she praised EU and Australian age rules while insisting addictive design harms adults too.

Her constructive example is Rappler Communities, a Matrix-based app the newsroom opened in 2023 so readers could talk to the desk and to each other without living inside a engagement farm. She wants that model to travel across Southeast Asian outlets the way cities once built parks: as public works for speech that can still listen. That is a small architecture next to a frontier model that books flights and moves money. It is also a reminder that agency is a civic noun before it is a product feature.

The same week, Anthropic's Dario Amodei asked labs to [pace the frontier together](/article/the-problem-with-letting-ai-labs-pace-the-frontier-together), and Microsoft posted a Humanist code that tells models they are not people. Those documents argue over brakes and personhood inside the lab. Ressa argues over who forces the law when the third wave starts acting for the public without a vote. Her three-phase map is journalism's way of saying the story already moved: attention was the opening theft, intimacy was the middle, and agency is the closing act unless legislation arrives first.

Ressa's test is blunt enough to keep. If a system can act for you, someone owes you a statute before the tip. Lab pledges and consultation drafts are optional literature until they bind holdouts. Citizens campaigning for rules are the load-bearing piece in her account. The frontier will keep shipping agents either way.
